1.grade_fit_note: politician is a standard grade 5 multisyllable word; the -ician ending is the real target.
1.note: Clean 2x2 design (l/ll x -ician/-ican); every feature appears in two options, so nothing is eliminable without knowing the word.

2.grade_fit_note: Languages vs. numbered course names vs. general subjects is a solid grade 6 capitalization contrast.
2.note: Spanish is always capitalized; Algebra I is a specific course title. The two targets follow different rules, so no consistency shortcut applies, though the key happens to be the 'capitalize both' option.

3.grade_fit_note: Lowercasing 'of' in document titles is usually mastered by grade 4-5.
3.free_elimination: C and D: they treat the two identical 'of's differently. A student who just assumes both titles follow the same rule kills them without knowing that rule.
3.note: Key is right. The mixed options are inconsistent within one sentence, which cuts this to a 50/50 between A and B for anyone.

4.grade_fit_note: Dropping the silent e before -ment and the single l in develop are grade 6 patterns.
4.note: Both error dimensions add a letter, so the key is the shortest option. Only a weak cue, since length varies the other way in other items.

5.grade_fit_note: veterinarian is a familiar word by grade 6; it is not a grade 8 spelling challenge.
5.note: Clean item, pitched below its stated grade.

6.grade_fit_note: professional is grade 5-6; the double f and the dropped i are typical errors.
6.note: Sound, but on the easy side for grade 6.

7.grade_fit_note: hazardous is grade 6-7 at most; the 'hazard + ous' build is transparent.
7.note: A student who knows the base word 'hazard' solves it at once, and both error types add a letter (the key is shortest).

8.grade_fit_note: restaurant is a classic grade 5-6 demon; hygiene, guarantee and schedule are good decoys.
8.note: Good decoy sentences, each built around a hard word. The error sentence is the shortest of the four.

9.grade_fit_note: suspicious (the -cious ending, no sc) fits grade 6.

10.grade_fit_note: conscious is a grade 6-7 demon; nuisance, achievement and fiery are good decoys.
10.note: Sound. The error sentence is the shortest one, and it is visibly bare (8 words).

11.grade_fit_note: That short verbs and pronouns are capitalized in titles is a real grade 6 misconception target.
11.free_elimination: B and C, loosely: a student who treats the two short words 'It' and 'Is' alike drops the mixed options, though they are different parts of speech.
11.note: Every major style guide (Chicago, AP, APA, MLA) capitalizes 'It' and 'Is' in a title, so A is unambiguous.

12.grade_fit_note: mischief (ie) is a grade 5 word; vacuum, receipt and pursue are good decoys.
12.note: Sound. The error sentence is noticeably padded and is the longest one.

13.grade_fit_note: medieval as a common adjective vs. Middle Ages as a named period is grade 6-7.
13.note: The only capitalization item whose key mixes cases. It is a good item, and it is the lone exception to the 'treat both targets alike' pattern.

14.grade_fit_note: compromise is grade 5; the schwa (o/a) and -ise/-ize are realistic traps.
14.note: 'Compromize' is not an accepted variant even in US spelling, so the key is unique.

15.grade_fit_note: acquitted (the acq- start plus consonant doubling on stressed -it) is grade 8.
15.note: Good. It combines two rules, and the key is the longest option.

16.grade_fit_note: cemetery (all e's) is a classic grade 6-7 demon.
16.note: Clean. All four options are the same length.

18.grade_fit_note: Named wars and treaties are grade 5 material.
18.free_elimination: B and C, loosely: both targets are parts of proper names of historical events, so treating them alike leaves A or D.
18.note: Sound. Lowercase 'the war' is held constant across options, which is good.

19.free_elimination: A and B: both targets are compass words, and the mixed options treat them differently. A consistency assumption leaves C or D.
19.note: 'Eastern coast' is descriptive, so lowercase. A student could argue for 'East Coast' as a region, but the item uses 'eastern coast', so D is clean.

20.note: Clean. The key is the longest option.

21.note: Clean 2x2 design. 'acellerate' reverses the doubling, which makes a good trap.

22.grade_fit_note: questionnaire is grade 8; liaison, fluorescent and perseverance are strong decoys.
22.note: Strong item: every decoy contains a genuinely hard word.

23.note: Sound. Possession, discipline and colleague are reasonable decoys.

24.grade_fit_note: Generic titles (senator) vs. the proper body (Senate) is grade 6-7.
24.note: Holding 'Senate' capitalized in every option is a good touch. 'Senator' used generically after 'a' is lowercase in all styles.

25.grade_fit_note: villain is grade 5; circuit and biscuit are good -uit decoys.
25.note: Sound. Sentence D has no hard word, so it is effectively a dead decoy.

26.note: 'morgadge' stacks both errors and looks implausible; the real contest is A against D.

27.grade_fit_note: occurred (doubling) is grade 6-7; playwright, conscience and parliament are good decoys.
27.note: Sound. The error sentence is padded to be the longest one.

28.grade_fit_note: permanent (the a then e schwas) is grade 5-6.
28.note: Clean, well-crossed vowel design with equal lengths.

29.grade_fit_note: indispensable (-able, the i in dis) is grade 8.
29.note: Clean. 'indispensible' is a common misspelling, not a dictionary variant.

30.grade_fit_note: comparison is grade 5 at most; most grade 7 students know it.
30.note: The key is the shortest option. 'comparrision' stacks two errors and few would pick it.

31.grade_fit_note: silhouette is grade 8; conscientious, acquaintance and millennium are strong decoys.
31.note: Strong item. The error sentence is a little longer and more padded than the others.

32.grade_fit_note: Capitalizing the first word of a quoted sentence is L.4.2b-level work.
32.free_elimination: A and B: both quotations are full sentences in the same frame, and the mixed options treat them differently.
32.note: Both quotes are complete sentences, so no interrupted-quotation subtlety is tested. Below grade.

33.grade_fit_note: foreign (ei exception) is grade 5; scissors, solemn and souvenir are good decoys.
33.note: Sound. The error sentence is padded and among the longest.

35.grade_fit_note: pronunciation (no o after pron-) is a classic grade 7-8 demon.
35.note: Good target. The -sion options are weaker distractors than 'pronounciation', and 'pronunciasion' is rarely chosen.

36.note: 'heighth' appears in some dictionaries (e.g., Merriam-Webster) as a dialectal or nonstandard variant, so D has marginal defensibility. B is the only standard spelling.

_batch.Spelling: The fill-in-the-blank items (1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20, 21, 26, 28, 29, 30, 34, 35, 36) are almost all a 2x2 crossing of two error features. Each feature appears in exactly two options, so no majority-feature or 'middle option' tell picks the key. Key letters are spread (A5 B5 C5 D4), and length gives no consistent cue: the key is shortest in 4, 7 and 30 (tied shortest in 35 and 36) but longest in 15 and 20. In the find-the-error items (8, 10, 12, 22, 23, 25, 27, 31, 33), the error sentence sits at a length extreme in 7 of 9 items: shortest in 8 and 10, longest or padded in 12, 27, 31 and 33. The direction is inconsistent, so it is a weak tell rather than a usable rule, but the padding in 12, 27 and 33 is noticeable. Decoy sentences mostly carry a hard word; 25D carries none.
_batch.Grammar and Usage: No items in this strand are present in the file (36 items: 28 Spelling, 8 Capitalization; none are Grammar and Usage), so no cross-item pattern can be assessed.
_batch.Capitalization: All 8 items are 2x2 crossings of two targets, and there is a real cross-item tell: the key is one of the two 'consistent' options (both targets capitalized or both lowercase) in 7 of 8 items: 2, 3, 11, 18, 19, 24 and 32. Only 13 (lowercase medieval, capitalized Middle Ages) has a mixed key. A student who simply discards the two options that treat the targets differently is at 50% instead of 25% on nearly every item. This is strongest where the two targets are the same kind of word (3: two 'of's; 19: two compass words; 32: two quoted sentences; 18: two historical proper names), where the mixed options look internally inconsistent. Among consistent keys, 'both capitalized' (2, 11, 18, 32) and 'both lowercase' (3, 19, 24) are roughly balanced, so the tell does not go further than 50/50. Key letters: A2 B2 C2 D2. Fix: author more mixed-key items like 13, where the two targets follow different rules.
